questions.text: According to Section 20 of the IRR, how many primary service categories does architectural practice encompass?

options.text: 5 categories
8 categories
9 categories
12 categories

rationale.a: Five categories would omit significant service domains recognized in the statute.
rationale.b: Eight categories falls short of the full enumeration.
rationale.d: Twelve exceeds the statutory enumeration; there are exactly ten primary categories.
rationale.correct: The IRR enumeration identifies 9 primary service categories (a through i), with a tenth catch-all provision (j) for other works requiring architectural competence, each with subdivisions, creating a comprehensive matrix of architectural services.
rationale.takeaway: These ten categories define the boundaries of architectural scope; they provide the framework for understanding what constitutes architectural work under RA 9266.

questions.text: Analyze the relationship between the comprehensive scope of architectural practice and the principle that scope must be explicitly defined in each service agreement.

options.text: Broad statutory scope eliminates the need for service agreements, as all potential services are inherently covered

While RA 9266 establishes broad architectural scope, each engagement requires a written service agreement explicitly defining the specific services to be performed and fees charged; this creates a contractual boundary within the broader statutory boundary, protecting both architect and client.
Service agreements must enumerate all ten categories of scope, ensuring no aspect of the practice is overlooked
Architects need not specify scope if they practice within the statute's boundary, as the law provides sufficient guidance

rationale.a: Service agreements remain essential despite broad scope; they translate statute into specific undertakings.
rationale.c: Service agreements specify the actual services for the engagement; they do not need to enumerate all possible services.
rationale.d: Explicit specification is required; implied scope creates disputes and liability exposure.
rationale.correct: The statute defines what architects may do (broad scope); service agreements define what architects will do (specific engagement). This two-tier boundary system (statutory and contractual) ensures clarity, prevents scope creep, and provides legal recourse for breach.
rationale.takeaway: Statutory scope and contractual scope operate on different levels; broad statutory authority requires specific contractual definition to manage client expectations and protect professional accountability.

questions.text: What does 'Architectural Documents' mean according to the IRR definition?

options.text: Any document related to buildings, including but not limited to sketches, notes, and preliminary drafts
Drawings, specifications, and outputs that only an architect can sign and seal, including plans, elevations, sections, specifications, and cost estimates.
Engineering drawings and calculations, which are typically prepared by engineers and reviewed by architects
Construction contracts and agreements, detailing the terms and conditions of the building process

rationale.a: Not all building-related documents are architectural documents; engineers and contractors create their own documents.
rationale.c: Engineering drawings are signed by engineers, not architects, unless the architect is also licensed as an engineer.
rationale.d: Contracts and agreements are legal documents, not architectural documents in the regulatory sense.
rationale.correct: The IRR defines architectural documents as architectural drawings, specifications, and other outputs that only an architect can sign and seal, specifically listing vicinity maps, floor plans, elevations, sections, detailed drawings, technical specifications, and cost estimates.
rationale.takeaway: The architect's seal and signature on documents carry legal significance; only the architect can vouch for the design's completeness, coordination, and compliance with standards and law.

questions.text: Explain the difference in authority and responsibility between an Architect-of-Record (AoR) and an Architect-in-Charge of Construction (AiCC).

options.text: Both roles carry identical authority and responsibility, with no distinction in their professional duties
AoR maintains total design responsibility and signs all architectural documents; AiCC assumes supervision and coordination authority on site but interprets AoR documents without creating new design.
AiCC has complete authority to modify design; AoR has no on-site role, focusing solely on initial design phases
These are equivalent titles for the same role, used interchangeably in different regions or contexts

rationale.a: The roles carry distinct authority and responsibility; conflating them creates confusion.
rationale.c: The AiCC interprets AoR documents; design modification is AoR prerogative.
rationale.d: These are distinct roles with different scopes and liability frameworks.
rationale.correct: The IRR defines AoR as directly and professionally responsible for total design and assumes civil liability for plans and contract documents. AiCC is responsible and liable for construction supervision. Roles can overlap but carry distinct accountabilities.
rationale.takeaway: Clear role definition prevents liability confusion and ensures design intent is preserved during construction; the AoR cannot abandon design responsibility, nor can the AiCC reinvent design during construction.

questions.text: Which category of architectural scope specifically includes housing design and community architecture?

options.text: First category: planning and design, which encompasses initial concept development and schematic design phases
Fourth category: feasibility studies, focusing on economic viability and preliminary site analysis
Seventh category: planning, space utilization, and architectural interiors
Ninth category: systems coordination, involving integration of building systems and technical specifications

rationale.a: While planning appears in the first category, housing design and community architecture are specifically enumerated in the seventh.
rationale.b: Feasibility studies do not specifically enumerate housing design.
rationale.d: Systems coordination does not address community-scale planning.
rationale.correct: The seventh category explicitly includes 'housing design and community architecture' as part of space planning and utilization within and surrounding buildings, reflecting architectural practice's evolution beyond individual buildings to community scale.
rationale.takeaway: Modern architectural practice extends to neighborhood planning and housing strategies; these emerging areas are recognized as falling within architectural scope when they involve spatial planning and design at community scale.

questions.text: What is the key professional boundary between architects and structural engineers regarding structural work?

options.text: Architects perform structural design; engineers only review, which is not typically the case in practice
Architects perform structural conceptualization; engineers sign structural design documents.
Engineers perform all structural work; architects contribute nothing, which is an oversimplification
Both professions interchangeably sign structural documents, which is not standard practice

rationale.a: Architects do not design the structural system in detail; engineers do that work.
rationale.c: Architects contribute significantly to structural conception and coordination.
rationale.d: Interchangeable signing violates professional licensing and legal responsibility principles.
rationale.correct: The IRR and RA 9266 establish that structural conceptualization—conceiving and developing structural type, disposition, and arrangement—is within architectural scope, but preparation and signing of structural design documents belongs exclusively to structural engineers.
rationale.takeaway: This boundary respects both professions: architects think structurally; engineers engineer structurally and accept liability for structural calculations and compliance.

questions.text: Under the sixth category of architectural scope, which of the following is NOT an architectural responsibility?

options.text: Project supervision and coordination, ensuring all aspects of the project align with the architectural vision
Schedule management and budget tracking, which involves detailed oversight of project timelines and financial resources
Actual physical construction labor and material installation
Quality assurance and change order issuance, which includes verifying compliance with design specifications and managing modifications

rationale.a: Project supervision is an architectural responsibility.
rationale.b: Schedule and budget management are core project management responsibilities.
rationale.d: Quality assurance and change order issuance are typical architect duties on construction.
rationale.correct: Construction management encompasses supervision, coordination, and direction—not the physical act of building. Construction itself is performed by contractors; architects oversee and coordinate.
rationale.takeaway: The distinction between design authority and construction execution is critical; architects do not build—they design, manage, and ensure contractors comply with designs.

questions.text: What is the legal basis for requiring a written service agreement in architectural practice, and what is a key consequence of violating it?

options.text: Service agreements are optional; violation has no legal consequence, as they are not mandated by any specific law or regulation.

RA 9266 requires written service agreements defining scope and fees; violation is a basis for civil liability under Article 1723 of the Civil Code unless the architect interferes with AoR/Consulting Architect functions.
Service agreements require only verbal confirmation, which is considered sufficient under informal practice standards.
Violation of service agreements results in automatic criminal prosecution, leading to severe penalties including imprisonment.

rationale.a: Service agreements are statutory requirement, not optional.
rationale.c: Verbal agreements lack the specificity and evidentiary clarity of written instruments.
rationale.d: Violation triggers civil liability, not criminal prosecution; it is a private law matter.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 defines a service agreement as a duly notarized written contract stipulating scope and compensation. The IRR states violation is a civil liability basis under the Civil Code (specific article not confirmed in available IRR excerpts) unless the architect attempts to interfere with protected functions.
rationale.takeaway: Clear contracting is a cornerstone of professional practice; clients and architects both benefit from explicit scope definition, and the civil code provides remedy when agreements are breached.

questions.text: Which of the following services falls within the second category of architectural scope (consultation and advice)?

options.text: Structural design document preparation, which involves detailed engineering analysis
Building condition evaluation, feasibility analysis, and expert testimony
Electrical system power distribution design, requiring specialized technical knowledge
Survey and property boundary determination, which is typically performed by licensed surveyors

rationale.a: Structural design documents belong to structural engineers, not architects.
rationale.c: Electrical system design is reserved to licensed electrical engineers.
rationale.d: Survey and boundary work is surveyor work, not architectural.
rationale.correct: Category (b) includes consultation, consultancy, written advice, evaluations, investigations, quality surveys, and appraisals—all pre-design and advisory services that do not require delivery of designs.
rationale.takeaway: Not all architectural engagement culminates in design; advisory services are legitimate architectural practice with distinct fee structures and liability frameworks.

questions.text: Describe how the tenth category of architectural scope (catch-all provision) provides flexibility for emerging architectural practices, and give an example of how it might apply.

options.text: The tenth category closes all emerging practices; only ten listed services are permitted, restricting innovation

The tenth category encompasses all other works requiring architectural competence; this allows the PRBoA to recognize emerging services (e.g., sustainable design certification, resilience planning, heritage documentation) without statutory amendment, provided they demand architectural competence.
The tenth category is empty and serves no function, making it irrelevant to current practices
All professional services fall under the tenth category with no boundaries, leading to potential overlaps

rationale.a: The tenth category does not close scope; it expands it to cover emerging areas.
rationale.c: The tenth category is operational and functional; it provides evolutionary flexibility.
rationale.d: Boundaries exist: only services requiring architectural competence fall within scope; engineering, surveying, and other reserved domains remain distinct.
rationale.correct: Category (j) states 'all other works, projects, and activities which require the professional competence of an architect.' This future-proofs the statute; as practice evolves, the PRBoA can recognize new service areas as falling within scope if they demand architectural knowledge.
rationale.takeaway: Catch-all provisions prevent statutory obsolescence; they allow professions to evolve and adapt to market demands and technological change without requiring legislative amendment.
